summary: Chinese word order is fixed, and it carries much of the grammar: subject – (time) – (place) – verb – object. The place, with 在, comes before the verb: 我在家吃饭 ‘I eat at home’ — never after it. The small words that modify the verb — 不 and 没 (S08), 都, 也 and 只 (S09) — stand right before it (or before 在 + place): 我们都不喝啤酒 ‘none of us drinks beer’. A topic can open the sentence: 早饭我吃面包 or 我早饭吃面包 ‘for breakfast I have bread’. Questions keep the same order (S09, S10).

blocks.title: The place does not follow the verb
blocks.text: ‘I eat at home’ is 我在家吃饭 — *我吃饭在家, with the place after the verb, is wrong.

blocks.title: Adverbs stick to the verb
blocks.text: 都 ‘all’, 也 ‘also’, 只 ‘only’, 不 and 没 stand right before the verb, or before 在 + place: 我们都在家吃饭 ‘we all eat at home’, 他不在家吃饭 ‘he doesn’t eat at home’.

blocks.title: Topic first
blocks.text: Something already in the conversation can open the sentence: 早饭我吃面包 / 我早饭吃面包 ‘breakfast — I have bread’. The rest keeps its order.

blocks.title: Before the verb: everything that frames the action
blocks.text: Time, place and the small adverbs come before the verb; only the object follows it: 我今天在家吃饭 ‘I eat at home today’.

askYourself: Who? → first (a topic or a time word may come before it).
When? → a time word before the verb, before or after the subject (S14).
Where? → 在 + place before the verb.
Is there 不, 没, 都, 也 or 只? → right before the verb (or before 在 + place).
What? → the object after the verb.
steps: adverb (不 / 都 / 也 / 只)

traps: *我吃饭在家 → 我在家吃饭.
*我们喝都茶 → 我们都喝茶.
German V2 does not apply: *今天吃我面包 → 今天我吃面包.

notes.text: Greek is SVO but very free (Το ψωμί το τρώω εγώ) and puts place and time after the verb (τρώω στο σπίτι); Chinese order is fixed, and place and time come before the verb: 我在家吃饭.
Russian order is free because case shows the roles; Chinese order is fixed because nothing else shows them. Я ем дома ‘I eat at home’ becomes 我在家吃饭 — the place moves in front of the verb.
Spanish is SVO with place and time usually after the verb (como en casa); Chinese puts them before it: 我在家吃饭.
English is SVO too, but puts place and time at the end (I eat at home today); Chinese puts them before the verb (我今天在家吃饭). *我吃饭在家 is the typical mistake.
French is SVO with place and time after the verb (je mange à la maison); Chinese: 我在家吃饭. French object pronouns go before the verb (je le mange); Chinese ones stay after it.
German V2 moves the verb to second place (Heute esse ich zu Hause); Chinese never moves it: 今天我在家吃饭. German puts the place after the verb; Chinese before it.
Hindi puts time and place before the verb too (मैं घर पर खाना खाता हूँ), like Chinese; but the Hindi object also precedes the verb (SOV), while the Chinese one follows it: 我在家吃饭.
Persian puts time and place before the verb (man dar khāne ghazā mikhoram) — the Chinese position — and the object too; Chinese puts the object after the verb.
Marathi puts time, place and object all before the verb (मी घरी जेवतो ‘I eat at home’); Chinese agrees for time and place (我在家吃饭) but puts the object after the verb.
Arabic puts the verb or the subject first (akala l-waladu / al-waladu akala) and the place after the verb (fī l-bayt); Chinese fixes subject – place – verb – object.
Hebrew is SVO with the place after the verb (ani okhel ba-bayit); Chinese puts it before: 我在家吃饭.
Turkish also puts time and place before the verb (Ben evde yemek yerim ‘I eat at home’); Chinese differs in putting the object after the verb: 我在家吃饭.
Japanese puts time and place before the verb, as Chinese does (家でご飯を食べる), and has a topic slot (は), like the Chinese topic first. But the Japanese object precedes the verb; the Chinese one follows.
Korean, like Chinese, puts time and place before the verb (집에서 밥을 먹어요) and has a topic slot (은 / 는); unlike Chinese, the object also precedes the verb.
Finnish is SVO but freer, with place and time often after the verb (syön kotona); Chinese fixes them before the verb: 我在家吃饭.
Hungarian order follows focus — the stressed element goes right before the verb; Chinese order follows the roles and is fixed: subject – time – place – verb – object.
Swahili is SVO with place and time after the verb (ninakula nyumbani ‘I eat at home’); Chinese puts them before: 我在家吃饭.
Luganda is SVO with the place after the verb; Chinese puts place and time before the verb and only the object after it.
Vietnamese is SVO like Chinese but usually puts the place after the verb (tôi ăn cơm ở nhà); Chinese says 我在家吃饭 — same type of language, opposite position.
Inuktitut packs subject and object into the verb word, which usually comes last; Chinese builds the sentence from separate words in a fixed order: subject – time – place – verb – object.

seeAlso.note: German keeps the verb in second place and can front the object (Den Tee trinke ich) because the accusative shows the role; Chinese keeps subject – (time) – (place) – verb – object.
Arabic often starts with the verb (يَشْرَبُ الْوَلَدُ الشَّايَ ‘the boy drinks the tea’) and its case endings allow other orders; a Chinese sentence never starts with the verb in a statement.
Hebrew is subject – verb – object like Chinese, but the place usually follows the verb (אֲנִי אוֹכֵל בַּבַּיִת); Chinese puts it before: 我在家吃饭.
